title: API Design: REST, OpenAPI & GraphQL
summary: A good API is a contract, not just a pile of endpoints. This topic covers three ways to design that contract in Go: **REST** (resources as nouns, HTTP verbs, correct status codes, idempotency, versioning, pagination, and consistent error envelopes), **OpenAPI/Swagger** (describe the contract in a spec — spec-first with `oapi-codegen` or code-first with `swaggo/swag` annotations — and generate docs and typed stubs), and **GraphQL** (a single typed schema with `gqlgen`, resolvers, queries/mutations, and the N+1 problem you solve with dataloaders). The through-line: design the contract deliberately, then let tooling enforce it.

subtopics.title: Resources, nouns, and HTTP verbs
subtopics.explanation: REST models your domain as resources named with plural nouns (/users, /orders/{id}/items), and the HTTP verb expresses the action: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, DELETE removes. Verbs stay out of the URL — you never write /getUser or /createOrder. Modeling nouns + verbs correctly is the first design decision that makes an API predictable, because clients can guess endpoints from the resource shape alone.

subtopics.title: Status codes & idempotency
subtopics.explanation: The status code IS part of your API: 200 for a read, 201 with a Location header for a create, 204 for a successful delete with no body, 400 for a bad request, 404 for a missing resource, 409 for a conflict, 422 for a validation failure. PUT and DELETE must be idempotent — repeating them yields the same server state — while POST is not, which is why retries and CDNs treat them differently. Returning the right code and honoring idempotency is what lets clients retry safely and reason about failures.

subtopics.title: Versioning & filtering
subtopics.explanation: Contracts change, so you version them — usually a URL prefix (/v1/users) for a clean break, sometimes a header or media type for finer control — and you never make a breaking change inside an existing version. Read-collection endpoints also accept query parameters for filtering, sorting, and field selection (?status=active&sort=-created_at) so clients fetch exactly what they need. Versioning plus expressive query filters lets an API evolve for years without breaking the clients already built against it.

subtopics.title: Cursor-based pagination
subtopics.explanation: Offset pagination (?page=3&limit=20 -> OFFSET 40) is simple but drifts: inserts shift rows so clients skip or repeat items, and deep offsets are slow because the DB still scans skipped rows. Cursor pagination encodes the last-seen key (an opaque token like the last id or created_at) and asks for rows after it, giving stable, index-friendly paging over changing data. For any large or fast-changing collection, cursor pagination is the correct default because it stays consistent and O(limit) no matter how deep the client reads.

subtopics.title: OpenAPI: spec-first vs code-first
subtopics.explanation: OpenAPI is a machine-readable description of your REST contract. Code-first tools like swaggo/swag read // @annotations on your handlers and emit the spec plus a Swagger UI, keeping docs next to code. Spec-first tools like oapi-codegen invert it: you author the openapi.yaml, then generate typed Go request/response structs and a server interface you implement, so the compiler enforces the contract. Whichever direction you pick, OpenAPI turns the contract into an artifact that generates docs, client SDKs, and mock servers instead of drifting prose.

subtopics.title: GraphQL, the N+1 problem, and dataloaders
subtopics.explanation: GraphQL exposes one typed schema where the client asks for exactly the fields it wants in a single request, resolved field-by-field by resolver functions. That per-field resolution creates the N+1 problem: fetching 100 posts then resolving each post's author fires 1 query for the posts plus 100 for authors. A dataloader fixes it by batching the keys requested within a tick and issuing one bulk query (WHERE id IN (...)), then caching per-request. GraphQL beats REST when clients need flexible, aggregated reads across many resources, but only once you've added dataloaders — otherwise its convenience quietly multiplies your database load.

foundations.overview: API design is the discipline of turning a domain into a stable, discoverable contract that clients can build against and you can evolve. REST does this with resources, verbs, and status codes over HTTP; OpenAPI captures that contract as a spec you can generate docs and code from; GraphQL replaces many fixed endpoints with one flexible typed graph. In Go you can implement all three with mature, idiomatic tooling — net/http or Gin for REST, oapi-codegen/swaggo for OpenAPI, and gqlgen for GraphQL — and the design choices (status codes, idempotency, versioning, pagination, N+1) matter far more than the framework.
foundations.formalDefinition: REST is an architectural style constraining an API to stateless, uniform-interface operations on addressable resources identified by URIs and manipulated via HTTP methods with standardized semantics and status codes. OpenAPI is a language-agnostic JSON/YAML schema describing those resources, operations, parameters, and responses. GraphQL is a query language and runtime where a typed schema defines fields resolved individually by resolver functions against arbitrary client-specified selection sets.
foundations.whyItMatters: The API is the product's public surface: a well-designed contract is self-explanatory, retry-safe, and evolvable, while a bad one leaks implementation details, breaks clients on every change, and multiplies support load. Interviewers probe API design because it reveals whether you think about contracts, failure modes, and scale — not just endpoints.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of REST as a well-organized library: every book (resource) has a fixed shelf address (URI), and standard actions (borrow/return = verbs) work the same on every book. OpenAPI is the library's catalog card describing each book so anyone can find and use it without opening it. GraphQL is a personal librarian: instead of walking fixed aisles, you hand over one detailed request ('these fields of these books, plus each author's birth year') and get exactly that back in one trip — powerful, but you must tell the librarian to fetch authors in one batch or they'll make a separate trip per book (the N+1 problem).
foundations.runtimePerspective: A REST request in Go dispatches through a router to a handler that reads path/query params, does work, and writes a status code plus JSON body — one round trip per resource. A GraphQL request hits a single endpoint; the runtime walks the query tree calling a resolver per field, which is where uncontrolled per-field database calls explode into N+1 unless a dataloader batches them within an execution tick. Generated OpenAPI stubs add no runtime cost — they're just typed structs and interfaces the compiler checks.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Public REST/JSON APIs (Stripe, GitHub) with versioned paths and cursor pagination; internal microservices described by OpenAPI so teams generate typed clients; mobile/BFF layers using GraphQL to let clients fetch tailored payloads in one request; and Swagger UI served straight from swaggo annotations for internal docs.
foundations.businessImpact: A clear, versioned contract lets external developers integrate in hours instead of days and lets you ship changes without breaking partners — directly affecting adoption and churn. Consistent error envelopes and correct status codes reduce failed integrations and support tickets; efficient pagination and dataloaders keep infra cost flat as clients scale.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Spec-first OpenAPI makes the contract the source of truth so client and server stay in sync via generated code, eliminating a whole class of integration bugs. Consistent conventions (nouns, status codes, error shape) let engineers work across services without relearning each one. GraphQL centralizes read shaping but shifts complexity into resolver performance, which the team must own.
foundations.performanceImpact: Cursor pagination keeps list endpoints O(limit) regardless of depth, unlike offset scans that degrade linearly. Field selection (REST sparse fields or GraphQL selection sets) cuts payload size and DB work. The dominant GraphQL performance risk is N+1 query fan-out; dataloaders collapse it from N+1 queries to a small constant, often a 10-100x reduction in DB calls on list-of-parents-with-children queries.
commonUseCases: Versioned REST/JSON APIs with cursor pagination and a consistent error envelope
Generating typed server/client stubs from an OpenAPI spec with oapi-codegen
Serving live Swagger UI docs from swaggo/swag handler annotations
A gqlgen GraphQL API with dataloaders to batch child-entity fetches

commonMisconceptions.reality: REST requires resource-oriented URIs, correct verb semantics, and standardized status codes. Endpoints like POST /getUserById that ignore verbs and always return 200 are RPC-over-HTTP, not REST.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Offset pagination (?page=N) is fine for everything.
commonMisconceptions.reality: On large or changing datasets it drifts (items skipped/repeated as rows shift) and deep offsets scan all skipped rows. Cursor pagination is stable and index-friendly for those cases.

commonMisconceptions.myth: GraphQL is always faster than REST because it's one request.
commonMisconceptions.reality: One request to the client can be N+1 queries on the server. Without dataloaders, resolving a list's child fields fans out into a query per item, often making GraphQL slower than a well-designed REST endpoint.

commonMisconceptions.myth: OpenAPI is just documentation you write after the fact.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Treated as the source of truth (spec-first), it generates typed server interfaces and client SDKs, so the compiler enforces the contract rather than prose drifting from code.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Returning 200 with an {"error": ...} body is acceptable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It breaks clients, proxies, and monitoring that key off status codes for retries and alerts. Errors must carry an appropriate 4xx/5xx status alongside the error envelope.

interactiveExamples.title: A consistent error envelope across a REST handler
interactiveExamples.explanation: Every error response should share one JSON shape and the correct status code so clients can parse failures uniformly. Here a small writeError helper sets the status and encodes a stable envelope, and the handler uses it for both 'not found' and validation cases.

code.caption: One helper keeps status codes and the error envelope consistent everywhere.
code.expectedOutput:
GET /users/  -> 400 {"error":{"code":"invalid_request","message":"id is required"}}
GET /users/9 -> 404 {"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"user does not exist"}}

interactiveExamples.title: Cursor pagination end to end
interactiveExamples.explanation: This handler implements the fetch-limit+1 trick: it asks the store for one more row than requested, and if it comes back it knows there's a next page and uses the last kept row's id as the opaque next_cursor. The response is stable even if rows are inserted between requests.

code.caption: fetch-limit+1 detects the next page without a separate COUNT query.

interactiveExamples.title: Batching a GraphQL resolver to eliminate N+1
interactiveExamples.explanation: This shows the shape of a per-request dataloader: the Author resolver never queries directly — it enqueues a key with Load, and a batch function receives every key collected in the execution tick and issues one IN-query. Compare the naive resolver (one query per post) to the batched one (one query total).

code.caption: Load() enqueues keys; the batch function turns N+1 into one IN-query.
code.expectedOutput:
// Naive, 3 posts:  3 separate SELECT ... WHERE id = ? queries
// Batched, 3 posts: SELECT * FROM users WHERE id IN [a b c]   (one query)

checkpoints.prompt: A client creates a resource with POST /users. Which status code and header combination is most correct?
options: 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource
204 No Content with the new body
checkpoints.explanation: A successful creation returns 201 Created and a Location header with the URI of the new resource (e.g. /users/42), optionally echoing the created entity in the body. 200 loses the 'created' semantics, 204 forbids a body, and 302 is a redirect, not a creation result.

checkpoints.prompt: A GraphQL query fetches 3 posts and each post's author, with NO dataloader. The author resolver runs one SQL query per call. How many total author queries fire?
options: 3 author queries (one per post) — the classic N+1
4 queries (posts + 3 authors) but that's fine and optimal
checkpoints.explanation: GraphQL resolves fields per object, so the Author resolver runs once for each of the 3 posts = 3 author queries, plus 1 for the posts list = the N+1 problem (here N=3). GraphQL does NOT batch automatically; a dataloader is what collapses those 3 into a single WHERE id IN (...) query.

checkpoints.prompt: This handler is meant to return 400 on a validation error, but clients always see 200 and a logging middleware records 200. What's the root cause?
options: ContentLength is unreliable so the branch never runs
w.Write is called before w.WriteHeader, so the status is implicitly 200 and the later WriteHeader(400) is ignored
You cannot return 400 from a POST handler
json must be used instead of Write
checkpoints.explanation: The first w.Write implicitly sends WriteHeader(200) because no status was set yet; the subsequent WriteHeader(400) is too late (and logs 'superfluous response.WriteHeader call'). Always set the status BEFORE writing the body — call w.WriteHeader(http.StatusBadRequest) first, or use http.Error which does both in the right order.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the idempotent replace: PUT should fully REPLACE the resource so repeating it leaves the same state. Fill in the correct verb registration.
checkpoints.explanation: PUT /users/{id} performs a full, idempotent replacement of a specific resource — sending it twice yields the same state. POST creates (not idempotent), PATCH partially updates, and GET reads. Idempotency is why clients and proxies can safely retry PUT and DELETE but not POST.

codeLab.title: Implement a cursor-based paginator
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Paginate(all []string, cursor string, limit int) (data []string, next string)`. Items are sorted strings acting as their own keys. Return up to `limit` items whose value is strictly greater than `cursor` (empty cursor = from the start), and set `next` to the last returned item's value IF more items remain after this page, otherwise "". Use the fetch-limit+1 technique.
hints: Collect items with value strictly greater than cursor; stop once you have limit+1 of them.
If you collected more than limit items, a next page exists: set next to data[limit-1], then slice data down to limit.
When you collected limit or fewer items, the list is exhausted, so next must stay "".

codeLab.title: Write a dataloader batch function
codeLab.instructions: Implement `BatchUsers(ids []string, db map[string]string) []*User` — the function a dataloader calls once with every key collected in a tick. Return a slice ALIGNED to ids (result[i] corresponds to ids[i]). If an id is missing from db, that position must be nil. This single call replaces the N per-item queries.
hints: Allocate out := make([]*User, len(ids)) so every position exists and defaults to nil.
Iterate ids with an index; look each id up in db with the comma-ok form.
Only set out[i] when the id is present; leave it nil otherwise so alignment and missing keys are both correct.

debuggingLab.title: API returns 200 on failure, breaking client retries
debuggingLab.symptom: A downstream service reports it never retries failed calls to this endpoint and its dashboards show a 100% success rate even during outages. The handler clearly hits its error branch, yet clients and monitoring see HTTP 200.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: json.NewEncoder(w).Encode writes to the response body, and the first write implicitly calls WriteHeader(200). Because the error branch never sets a 4xx/5xx status before writing, the client receives HTTP 200 with an error JSON body. Clients, proxies, and monitoring key their retry and alerting logic off the status code, so a 200 tells them 'success' — they never retry and dashboards report no errors. The error envelope in the body is invisible to that machinery.
commonMistakes: Encoding an error body without first calling w.WriteHeader with a 4xx/5xx status.
Assuming the presence of an 'error' field in the JSON is enough for clients to detect failure.
Setting the status code AFTER the first Write, which is ignored and logs 'superfluous response.WriteHeader call'.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Set the correct status code (e.g. 404 for not found) BEFORE writing the error envelope, so the status and body agree.

solution.expectedOutput: GET /orders/missing -> 404 {"error":"order not found"}   // clients now retry/alert correctly

theory.question: What makes an API RESTful, and how do HTTP verbs and status codes encode intent?
theory.directAnswer: A RESTful API models the domain as resources addressed by nouns in the URI (/users/{id}), uses HTTP verbs for the action (GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial update, DELETE remove), and returns standardized status codes (2xx success, 4xx client error, 5xx server error). Verbs never appear in the path, PUT/DELETE are idempotent while POST is not, and the status code is a first-class part of the contract that clients and infrastructure rely on for retries and caching. This uniform interface is what makes endpoints predictable without reading docs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An architectural style constraining APIs to stateless operations on addressable resources via a uniform HTTP interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A uniform, self-describing interface lets clients, caches, and proxies interoperate without per-API special-casing.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: URIs identify resources; the verb selects the operation with defined semantics; the status code reports the outcome; idempotent verbs are safely retryable.

theory.whyImportant: REST is the default shape of web APIs, and interviewers use it to check whether you think in contracts and failure modes rather than ad-hoc endpoints.
theory.realWorldExample: GitHub's API: GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues lists, POST creates (201 + Location), and DELETE removes (204) — verbs and codes carry the meaning.

followUps.question: When would you use PATCH instead of PUT?
followUps.answer: PATCH applies a partial update (only the fields sent) and is not required to be idempotent, while PUT replaces the entire resource and must be idempotent. Use PATCH when clients should modify a subset of fields.

followUps.question: Is returning 200 with an error body ever acceptable?
followUps.answer: No for REST — it breaks proxies, retries, and monitoring that key off status. GraphQL is the exception: it returns 200 with an errors array because it's a single endpoint with its own error model.

theory.question: Compare offset and cursor pagination. When is each appropriate?
theory.directAnswer: Offset pagination (?page=N&limit=L -> OFFSET N*L) is simple and allows jumping to arbitrary pages, but it drifts when rows are inserted or deleted (clients skip or repeat items) and gets slow at deep offsets because the DB scans all skipped rows. Cursor pagination sends an opaque token encoding the last-seen key and fetches rows after it (WHERE id > cursor ORDER BY id LIMIT L), giving stable results over changing data and O(limit) index seeks regardless of depth. Use offset for small, static datasets or admin UIs needing page numbers; use cursor for large, fast-changing, or infinite-scroll feeds.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two strategies for returning a large collection in bounded pages.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: APIs must return partial results to bound payload size and latency; how you slice affects correctness and performance.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Offset skips N rows before returning L; cursor seeks by an indexed key past the last-seen value, avoiding the skip scan.

theory.whyImportant: Pagination choice is a common source of duplicate/missing items and slow queries at scale, and it's a frequent design-interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: Twitter/X and Stripe expose cursor-based pagination (next_cursor / starting_after) precisely because their feeds change constantly and go arbitrarily deep.

followUps.question: How do you keep a cursor opaque and stable?
followUps.answer: Encode the sort key(s) (e.g. created_at + id) into a base64 token so clients treat it as opaque and you can change its internals; include a tiebreaker like id to make ordering deterministic.

followUps.question: How do you detect there's a next page without a COUNT?
followUps.answer: Fetch limit+1 rows; if you get the extra row, a next page exists and its predecessor becomes the next cursor. This avoids an expensive COUNT query.

theory.question: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how do dataloaders solve it?
theory.directAnswer: GraphQL resolves each field of each object with its own resolver function, so a query for a list of parents plus one child field per parent fires 1 query for the list and N queries for the children — the N+1 problem. A dataloader solves it by intercepting each child request: instead of querying immediately, the resolver calls Load(key), which enqueues the key; at the end of the execution tick the loader invokes one batch function with all collected keys and issues a single bulk query (WHERE id IN (...)), then distributes and per-request caches the results. This collapses N+1 into a small constant number of queries.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Per-field resolution causing redundant child queries, and the batching layer that coalesces them.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: GraphQL's flexible per-field model naturally produces fan-out; dataloaders were introduced (originally by Facebook) to batch and cache within a request.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Load enqueues keys during the tick; a single batch call fetches them all, returns results aligned to the keys, and caches per request to dedupe repeats.

theory.whyImportant: It's the defining performance pitfall of GraphQL; not handling it makes GraphQL slower than REST and is a guaranteed interview topic.
theory.realWorldExample: In gqlgen, a Post.Author resolver calls dataloader.For(ctx).UserByID.Load(id); 100 posts trigger one SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...) instead of 100 point queries.

followUps.question: Why must the batch function return results in the same order as the keys?
followUps.answer: The dataloader maps each returned element back to the caller by index/position, so misaligned results deliver the wrong entity to the wrong resolver; align by building output from the keys.

followUps.question: What is the scope of a dataloader's cache?
followUps.answer: Per request (per execution) — it's created fresh for each incoming GraphQL request and stored in the context, so stale data doesn't leak across requests.

scenario.question: Your public REST API must add a required field to a response and rename another, but thousands of existing integrations depend on the current shape. How do you roll this out without breaking clients?
scenario.directAnswer: Treat the change as breaking and version the contract rather than mutating v1. Introduce /v2 (URL versioning for a clean break) with the new/renamed fields, keep /v1 serving the old shape, and share the underlying service logic with a translation layer that maps the internal model to each version's representation. Announce a deprecation timeline for v1 with sunset headers, add metrics per version to watch migration, and only remove v1 once traffic drops near zero. Additive, non-breaking changes (a new OPTIONAL field) can go into v1 directly since well-behaved clients ignore unknown fields.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A backward-compatible evolution strategy for a public contract with many consumers.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Breaking changes to a live contract cause integration outages; versioning lets old and new coexist during migration.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A new version serves the new shape while the old version is frozen; a mapping layer reuses core logic; deprecation is signaled and measured before removal.

scenario.whyImportant: API evolution without breakage is core to platform trust and directly affects partner churn; interviewers use it to test contract discipline.
scenario.realWorldExample: Stripe pins each account to an API version and translates internally, so old integrations keep working for years while new features ship under newer versions.

followUps.question: When is a change NOT breaking, so no new version is needed?
followUps.answer: Adding an optional response field, adding a new optional request parameter, or adding a new endpoint — clients that ignore unknown fields are unaffected. Removing/renaming fields or changing types IS breaking.

followUps.question: How do you know when it's safe to remove v1?
followUps.answer: Track per-version request metrics and unique client identifiers; after the announced sunset date and once traffic is negligible, remove v1, ideally returning 410 Gone with guidance for a grace period.

scenario.question: A team wants to replace three chatty REST endpoints (feed, then per-item author, then per-item comments) with GraphQL to reduce mobile round trips. What do you advise, and what must be in place before shipping?
scenario.directAnswer: GraphQL is a good fit here: the client can request the feed plus each item's author and comments in one request with exactly the fields it needs, eliminating the three-round-trip waterfall and over-fetching that hurts mobile. But before shipping, insist on dataloaders for author and comments resolvers, or the single client request becomes N+1 queries on the server and you've moved the problem, not solved it. Also add query-complexity/depth limiting and persisted queries to prevent abusive deep queries, per-field authorization, and monitoring of resolver-level latency. If the access pattern were a single fixed shape, a well-designed REST endpoint (with sparse fieldsets) might be simpler.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A decision on adopting GraphQL to collapse a multi-request REST waterfall for a mobile client.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Mobile clients suffer from round-trip latency and over-fetching; GraphQL lets them fetch a tailored graph in one request.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: One query resolves the tree field-by-field; dataloaders batch child fetches; complexity limits and auth guard the flexible surface.

scenario.whyImportant: It tests whether you weigh GraphQL's flexibility against its operational costs rather than adopting it as a buzzword.
scenario.realWorldExample: Mobile BFFs (backend-for-frontend) at companies like GitHub and Shopify use GraphQL so each screen fetches its exact data in one request, backed by dataloaders and complexity limits.

followUps.question: When would REST be the better choice here?
followUps.answer: If clients need a single stable payload shape, want HTTP caching/CDN edge caching on GET, or the team lacks the ops maturity for query-cost control, REST with sparse fieldsets and includes is simpler and cache-friendly.

followUps.question: How do you stop a client from requesting an enormously deep/expensive query?
followUps.answer: Enforce max query depth and a complexity budget, use persisted (allow-listed) queries in production, and apply per-resolver timeouts so no single request can exhaust the backend.

systemDesign.question: Design the public API for a document-collaboration product in Go. It needs REST resources, an OpenAPI contract for third-party SDKs, cursor pagination, and a GraphQL layer for the web client. Walk through the design.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Model resources as nouns — /v1/documents, /v1/documents/{id}/comments, /v1/users — with correct verbs and codes (201+Location on create, 204 on delete, 404/409/422 on errors) and a single error envelope {error:{code,message,details}}. Make the OpenAPI spec the source of truth (spec-first) and generate the Go server interface and public client SDKs with oapi-codegen, serving Swagger UI for docs; the compiler then enforces that handlers match the contract. Paginate all collections with opaque cursors (base64 of created_at+id), using fetch-limit+1 to compute next_cursor without COUNT. Version via URL prefix and freeze older versions. Add a GraphQL endpoint (gqlgen) for the web client so it fetches a document plus its comments and authors in one request, backed by per-request dataloaders for authors/comments to avoid N+1, plus query depth/complexity limits and persisted queries. Cross-cutting: auth middleware (API keys for SDKs, session/JWT for web), per-request context propagation and timeouts, rate limiting keyed by client, structured logs with a request ID, and RED metrics per route/resolver. Share one service layer between the REST and GraphQL handlers so business logic isn't duplicated.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A layered API: a versioned REST surface described by OpenAPI plus a GraphQL layer, over a shared service core.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Third parties want stable typed REST/SDKs while the first-party web client benefits from GraphQL's flexible reads; both should reuse one contract-enforced service layer.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: OpenAPI generates typed REST stubs; gqlgen generates GraphQL resolvers using dataloaders; both call a shared service; cursors page collections; middleware handles auth/limits/observability.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It exercises every design lever at once — resource modeling, contract-as-code, pagination, GraphQL performance, and operability — which is exactly what senior API-design interviews probe.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: Products like Notion and Linear expose a versioned REST/OpenAPI API for integrations plus a GraphQL API powering their own web app, sharing core services underneath.

followUps.question: How do you keep REST and GraphQL from duplicating logic?
followUps.answer: Put all business rules and data access in a service/domain layer with plain Go types; REST handlers and GraphQL resolvers are thin adapters that call it and translate to their respective response shapes.

followUps.question: How do the SDKs stay in sync with the API?
followUps.answer: Because the OpenAPI spec is the source of truth, regenerating client SDKs from the updated spec on each release keeps them typed and current; CI fails if handlers don't satisfy the generated server interface.

followUps.question: How do you protect the GraphQL endpoint in production?
followUps.answer: Persisted (allow-listed) queries so clients can only send known documents, query depth and complexity limits, per-resolver timeouts, and dataloaders so even allowed queries stay efficient.

coding.question: Implement a helper `WriteJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, v any)` that writes any value as JSON with the correct Content-Type and status code, in the right order to avoid the 'superfluous WriteHeader' bug. Then show a getUser handler using it for both success and a 404.
coding.thoughtProcess: The core rule: set headers and status BEFORE writing the body, because the first Write implicitly sends 200. So WriteJSON sets Content-Type, calls WriteHeader(status), then encodes. Encoding directly to w streams the body. The handler calls WriteJSON(w, 200, user) on success and WriteJSON(w, 404, errorEnvelope) when the user is missing, so status and body always agree.
coding.lineByLine: WriteJSON first sets the Content-Type header (headers must be set before WriteHeader), then calls WriteHeader(status) to commit the status line, then json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v) streams the body — this ordering avoids the implicit 200 and 'superfluous WriteHeader' log. getUser looks up the user; on miss it calls WriteJSON with 404 and the standard error envelope so the status matches the body; on hit it returns 200 with the user. Both paths go through one helper, guaranteeing consistent headers and ordering everywhere.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the size of the serialized value v (the JSON encoding cost).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra — Encode streams directly to the ResponseWriter without buffering the whole payload.

followUps.question: Why encode directly to w instead of json.Marshal then Write?
followUps.answer: Encoding to w streams the body without allocating a full byte slice for large payloads; the trade-off is that if encoding fails mid-stream you can't change the already-sent status, so validate before writing when correctness matters.

followUps.question: How would you make WriteJSON return an error for the caller to handle?
followUps.answer: Return the Encode error: `return json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)`; but note the status is already sent, so the caller can only log it, not change the response status.

coding.question: Implement `EncodeCursor(createdAt, id string) string` and `DecodeCursor(token string) (createdAt, id string, err error)` for opaque, stable cursor pagination. The cursor must combine a sort timestamp and a tiebreaker id and be safe to expose to clients.
coding.thoughtProcess: Clients should treat cursors as opaque, so encode the composite key (created_at + a tiebreaker id) into a single base64 token; that lets me change the internal format later without breaking clients. Join the two fields with a delimiter unlikely to appear in the values (I'll use a null byte), base64url-encode the result for URL safety, and reverse the process on decode with validation that both parts are present.
coding.lineByLine: EncodeCursor joins createdAt and id with a null byte so the two composite-key parts can be split unambiguously, then base64.RawURLEncoding makes the token URL-safe and opaque (no padding, no +// characters). DecodeCursor treats an empty token as the collection start, base64-decodes with error wrapping so a garbage token yields a clean error, splits on the null byte into exactly two parts, and returns both fields. The composite key (timestamp + tiebreaker id) guarantees a total ordering so paging is deterministic even when many rows share a timestamp.
coding.timeComplexity: O(k) in the length of the encoded/decoded string.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(k) for the decoded byte slice and the split parts.

followUps.question: Why include the id as a tiebreaker alongside created_at?
followUps.answer: created_at can collide across rows; without a unique tiebreaker the ORDER BY isn't total and pages can overlap or skip rows. The id makes ordering deterministic so cursoring is stable.

followUps.question: Should you sign or encrypt the cursor?
followUps.answer: If exposing internal keys is a concern, HMAC-sign the payload so clients can't forge cursors to probe data, or encrypt it; base64 alone is encoding, not security.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Keep one service/domain layer with plain Go types and put REST handlers, GraphQL resolvers, and generated OpenAPI stubs on top as thin adapters, so business logic is never duplicated across protocols. Make the OpenAPI spec the source of truth (spec-first with oapi-codegen) so the compiler enforces the REST contract, and generate GraphQL resolvers with gqlgen from a schema. Version REST via URL prefix, freeze old versions, and expose docs (Swagger UI) and the GraphQL playground behind auth.
productionDeepDive.performance: Paginate every collection with cursors (fetch-limit+1, no COUNT) so list latency stays O(limit) at any depth. Support field selection (REST sparse fieldsets or GraphQL selection sets) to shrink payloads and DB work. In GraphQL, dataloaders are mandatory for any child-entity resolver — they turn N+1 into one IN-query and commonly cut DB calls 10-100x on list queries. Reuse one tuned http.Client for outbound calls and enable gzip on large JSON responses.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Each request runs in its own goroutine, so shared caches/loaders must be safe or scoped per request; dataloaders are created fresh per request and stored in the context precisely to avoid cross-request data bleed. Bound any handler fan-out with an errgroup/semaphore and always pass r.Context() into DB/RPC calls so client disconnects and timeouts cancel work.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Set explicit server timeouts (net/http has none by default) and per-request context deadlines so slow clients or dependencies can't pin resources. Return correct status codes so clients and proxies retry only idempotent, retriable failures. For GraphQL, enforce query depth/complexity limits and persisted queries so a single request can't overload the backend. Validate and size-limit request bodies with http.MaxBytesReader.
productionDeepDive.observability: Emit structured logs with a request ID propagated via context, and for GraphQL log at the resolver level so N+1 regressions are visible. Record RED metrics (Rate, Errors, Duration) per REST route and per GraphQL operation/resolver with latency histograms, and track a dataloader hit/batch ratio to catch missing batching. Instrument with OpenTelemetry so a slow query is traceable to the exact resolver or endpoint.
productionDeepDive.security: Authenticate in middleware (API keys or JWT) and authorize per resource/field — GraphQL needs field-level authorization since one query can traverse many entities. Never expose internal IDs or errors verbatim; return the safe error envelope and log details server-side. Rate-limit per client, set ReadHeaderTimeout against slow-loris, size-limit bodies, and in GraphQL use allow-listed persisted queries in production to prevent arbitrary expensive queries.

caseStudies.problem: Thousands of integrations must keep working for years while the API keeps evolving with new fields and behaviors.
caseStudies.solution: Pin each account to a dated API version and translate internally to the current model, with cursor-based pagination (starting_after) and a stable error object shape across the whole API.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Maintaining many versioned representations and translation layers adds engineering overhead, but it buys near-total backward compatibility and partner trust.
caseStudies.lessons: Treat the API as a long-lived contract: version deliberately, paginate with cursors, and keep error/response shapes consistent so clients can build durable integrations.

caseStudies.problem: A single fixed REST payload over- or under-fetched for the many different screens of their web and mobile clients, causing chatty round trips.
caseStudies.solution: Introduced a GraphQL API alongside REST so clients fetch exactly the fields they need in one request, backed by dataloaders to batch child fetches and query-cost limits to bound expense.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: GraphQL added resolver-performance and query-cost-control complexity that REST didn't have, and required dataloaders everywhere to avoid N+1.
caseStudies.lessons: GraphQL wins for flexible, client-tailored reads but only pays off when dataloaders and complexity limits are in place from day one; REST remains simpler and more cache-friendly for fixed shapes.

keyTakeaways: REST models the domain as nouns with HTTP verbs and correct status codes (201+Location on create, 204 on delete, 4xx/5xx on errors); PUT/DELETE are idempotent and safely retryable, POST is not.
Never return 200 on failure — clients, proxies, and monitoring key retries and alerts off the status code, so set the status BEFORE writing the body and pair it with a consistent error envelope.
Prefer cursor pagination (opaque token + fetch-limit+1) over offset for large or fast-changing collections: it stays consistent under inserts/deletes and O(limit) at any depth.

OpenAPI turns the contract into an artifact: spec-first with oapi-codegen generates typed server interfaces and client SDKs the compiler enforces, while code-first swaggo annotations keep Swagger docs next to handlers.
GraphQL's per-field resolution causes the N+1 problem; dataloaders batch keys collected in a tick into one IN-query and cache per request, collapsing N+1 into a small constant.
GraphQL beats REST for flexible, aggregated, client-tailored reads but only with dataloaders and query-complexity limits in place; REST stays simpler and more cache-friendly for fixed payload shapes.
